migrationNotes: Spine: sketch a walk as dots on a graph, then read it back stretch by stretch: a rising line is a steady move, a flat one a stop, a falling one a return, and the two ends give the average.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): phys-reading-motion-graphs-rise and -2. The slope question is covered by -1 and the pause by the self-explanation phys-reading-motion-graphs-flat-line.

lesson.title: Read a motion graph

lead.text: Here is how the sketch is drawn. Time runs along the horizontal axis, starting at 0 on the left. Position goes up the vertical axis, measured from the origin as in the first lesson. Each pair of readings from the table becomes one dot, placed above its time at the height of its position. A sketch made this way is called a position–time graph.

Take a walker who covers 2 metres every second. At 1 s the dot sits at 2 m. At 2 s it sits at 4 m, and at 3 s it sits at 6 m. The dots lie on a straight line, and that is no accident. When the position changes by the same amount each second, the dots line up. Joining them gives a straight line.

afterFigure.text: The second case in the picture is a faster walker, who covers 4 metres every second. The line is still straight, but it climbs more quickly. Keep an eye on how the line leans, because the lean carries the information in the rest of this lesson.

lead.text: Back to the friend in the corridor, who keeps a steady pace away from the door.

The lean of a line is called its slope, and here it has a simple meaning. Pick two points on a straight line. The rise is how far the line goes up between them, which is the change in position. The run is how far it goes along, which is the change in time. Slope is the rise divided by the run.

Change in position divided by change in time is the quantity from the last lesson: the velocity. So the slope of a position–time graph is the velocity. A line from 1 m at 0 s up to 10 m at 3 s rises 9 m over a run of 3 s, which gives a slope of 9 ÷ 3 = 3 m/s. A steeper line means a faster move.

afterFigure.text: The slope of a straight line is the same wherever you measure it, so you can pick whichever two points are easiest to read. That is what makes the graph a quick way to get a velocity. You read two points, subtract on each axis and divide.

lead.text: A straight line on a position–time graph runs from 2 m at 0 s up to 14 m at 3 s.

reveal.text: You divided the rise by the run. That quotient is the velocity along the segment.

lead.text: So far every line has climbed. Two other shapes matter. If the position stays at 6 m for a few seconds, the dots sit at the same height and the line runs flat. A flat line has a rise of zero, so its slope is zero. The object has stopped at that spot.

If the position gets smaller as time passes, the line slopes downwards. Take a line from 14 m at 0 s to 2 m at 4 s. The rise is 2 − 14 = −12 m over a run of 4 s, so the slope is −12 ÷ 4 = −3 m/s. The minus sign means the object is moving in the negative direction, back towards the origin.

afterFigure.text: One graph can now tell a whole story. The shoelace walk from the start of the lesson draws a line that rises while the friend sets off. It runs flat during the stop and falls on the way back. Reading a graph like this means going through it a stretch at a time and asking what the slope of each stretch is.

lead.text: A walker heads back towards the origin, so the line on the graph slopes down.

reveal.text: Final minus initial is negative, so the velocity is negative: motion in the negative direction.

steps.headline: A trolley is out for 2 s, still for 2 s and back for 2 s. Find its velocity in each stretch.

workedSteps.text: The first stretch rises from 0 m to 8 m in 2 s. Divide the rise by the run.
The middle stretch is flat, so the position holds.
The last stretch falls from 8 m to 2 m in 2 s.

steps.headline: One number for the whole trip

lead.text: A graph with several stretches has several velocities, but sometimes you want one number for the entire trip. That is the average velocity we met earlier, and the graph makes it easy to find. Look only at the first point and the last point, and ignore everything in between.

Suppose a walker starts at 1 m at 0 s and finishes at 7 m at 10 s, after a pause and a short detour on the way. The rise from end to end is 7 − 1 = 6 m over a run of 10 s, so the average velocity is 6 ÷ 10 = 0.6 m/s. The pause and the detour still use up time, and that is why the average is slow.

afterFigure.text: You do not need the middle of the graph for this. Displacement depends only on where the trip began and where it ended, so the end points are enough. The straight line in the picture has the same slope as the whole winding trip.

lead.text: The trolley from the worked example is back on the graph: out, a pause, then a return. Only its start, its finish and the total time matter for the average.

reveal.text: The pause and the turn still use up time, so they pull the average velocity down to 1/3 m/s.

lesson.orientation: Interpret a position–time graph as changing position, pauses and reversals.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A friend walks away from you down the corridor while you note where they are at each second. After 2 seconds they are 3 metres from the door. After 4 seconds they are at 6 metres. You jot each pair of numbers in a table, and by the end of a minute the table is long.

Two quite different walks could produce a table that long. One friend strolled steadily the whole way. The other set off briskly, stopped to tie a shoelace and then wandered back. Reading the rows one at a time to tell which walk you have is slow work, and it is easy to lose track of what the numbers are doing.

A sketch fixes that. Plot each reading as a dot and join the dots, and the shape of the line shows how the walk went. We'll learn to draw a trip that way and then to read its story back out of the shape.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read velocity from the slope of a position–time graph and spot pauses and turns.

recap.keyIdea: On a position–time graph, slope is velocity: steep is fast, flat is stopped and falling is negative. The average velocity of a whole trip needs only its end points.

blocks.text: You turned 3 m after 2 s into 9 m after 6 s, and read a flat stretch as a stop and a falling one as motion in the negative direction. Over a trip with a pause and a turn you found an average velocity of just 1/3 m/s.

recap.nextHook: So far the velocity has stayed fixed along each stretch. Next it starts to change, and we need a name for how quickly it does.

questions.prompt: A straight position–time segment goes from 2 m at 0 s to 14 m at 3 s. What velocity does it show, in m/s?
hints: Read the changes on both axes.
Divide position change by time change.
Calculate (14 − 2)/3.
questions.onCorrect: +4 m/s. Rise over run on a position–time graph is velocity.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the change in position only. Divide it by the time the change took.
That divides time by position. The slope is position change per unit time.

questions.prompt: A position–time graph is horizontal from 2 s to 4 s. What does the object do during that interval?
hints: Compare the position at the ends of the horizontal segment.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Position stays fixed during the interval, so the object is stationary.

choices.label: Moves at a positive constant speed

questions.onCorrect: Flat means the position does not change, so the object is at rest during that time.

misconceptions.feedback: Constant speed would need a line that rises or falls. This line stays at one height.
Accelerating would show a curve. A level line means no change in position at all.

questions.prompt: Position falls from 10 m to 2 m along a straight graph segment lasting 4 s. Find the velocity in m/s.
hints: A falling position reading has a negative change.
Use final position minus initial position.
Calculate (2 − 10)/4.
questions.onCorrect: −2 m/s. A falling position line means a negative velocity. Final minus initial, over the time.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the position is falling. The velocity has to be negative.
That is the change in position alone. Divide by the time it took.

questions.prompt: A graph starts at 0 m at 0 s and finishes at 2 m at 6 s, with a pause and reversal between. Find the overall average velocity in m/s; a fraction is accepted.
hints: Use the outer endpoints for the full interval.
Include the entire elapsed time, including the pause.
Divide 2 by 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Overall displacement is 2 m over 6 s: 2/6 = 1/3 m/s.

questions.onCorrect: 1/3 m/s. Use the outer endpoints and the whole time. The pause and the turn still count as time.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the position change by the wrong time. Use the full 6 seconds.
That drops the pause from the time. The time on the graph runs from start to finish.

questions.prompt: A straight graph segment runs from x = 3 m at t = 1 s to x = 15 m at t = 4 s. Find its velocity in m/s.
hints: Subtract the earlier reading from the later reading on each axis.
Subtract the earlier time from the later time.
Divide the change in position by the change in time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Position change is 12 m and time change is 3 s: 12/3 = 4 m/s.

questions.onCorrect: +4 m/s. Subtract on both axes, then divide: the change in position over the change in time.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the change in position. Divide by the change in time as well.
That divides the later position by the later time. Use the changes, not the readings.

questions.prompt: What does a straight rising line on a position–time graph indicate?
hints: A graph of position against time shows a rate, not the shape of the road.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Equal time intervals produce equal positive position changes, which is constant positive velocity.

questions.onCorrect: A straight rising line means equal position steps in equal times: constant positive velocity.

misconceptions.feedback: The graph plots position against time. It does not show the slope of a road.
Increasing velocity would bend the line upward. A straight line has one constant slope.

questions.prompt: A friend walks away from the door at a steady pace and is 3 m away after 2 s. How far from the door are they after 6 s, in metres?
hints: How many 2-second chunks fit into 6 seconds?
A steady pace adds the same amount to the position in every chunk.
Find what one chunk adds, then count the chunks.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 6 s is three lots of 2 s, so 3 × 3 = 9 m.

questions.onCorrect: 9 m. Equal times give equal steps in position, which is why a steady walk draws a straight line.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the extra time as only 3 m more. Each 2 s adds 3 m, so 6 s adds more than that.
That multiplies the distance by the time. Count how many 2 s chunks fit into 6 s.

questions.prompt: A straight position–time line passes through 4 m at 1 s and 10 m at 3 s. What is its slope in m/s?
hints: How much does the position change between the two points?
How much does the time change?
Divide the position change by the time change.
questions.onCorrect: 3 m/s. The slope of a position–time line is the velocity.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the change in position only. Divide it by the change in time.
That reads off a single point. Use the change between the two.

questions.prompt: Why does a flat stretch on this graph mean the object has stopped?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.

acceptedIdeas: Its position stays the same while time passes.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its position stays the same while time passes.

choices.label: Its position stays the same while time passes.
Its velocity is at its largest.

questions.onCorrect: The vertical axis is position, not height. A flat line means position is not changing.

misconceptions.feedback: The graph does not show the road. Its vertical axis is position along the track.
The slope of a flat line is zero, and the slope is the velocity.

questions.prompt: A position–time graph has one straight segment from 20 m at 0 s to 5 m at 3 s. What velocity does it show, in m/s?
hints: Is the position rising or falling?
Final position minus initial position, over the time.
Take 20 away from 5, then share it over the 3 s.
questions.onCorrect: −5 m/s. The line falls, so the velocity is negative.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the position falls. Show that with a sign.
That is the change in position. Divide it by the time as well.

citations.claim: A position–time graph plots position against time, and equal position changes in equal times give a straight line.
A steady walker who is 3 m away after 2 s is 9 m away after 6 s.
The slope of a position–time graph is rise over run, which is the change in position over the change in time: the velocity.
A segment from 2 m at 0 s to 14 m at 3 s has a slope of 12 ÷ 3 = 4 m/s.
A flat position–time line means the object is at rest, and a falling line means negative velocity.
A segment falling from 10 m to 2 m in 4 s has a slope of −8 ÷ 4 = −2 m/s.
A trolley that rises 8 m in 2 s, stays level for 2 s and falls 6 m in 2 s has velocities +4 m/s, 0 m/s and −3 m/s.
The average velocity of a trip is the slope between its first and last points on a position–time graph.
A trip from 0 m at 0 s to 2 m at 6 s has an average velocity of 2 ÷ 6 = 1/3 m/s.
Overall displacement is 2 m over 6 s: 2/6 = 1/3 m/s.
Position change is 12 m and time change is 3 s: 12/3 = 4 m/s.
Equal time intervals produce equal positive position changes, which is constant positive velocity.
6 s is three lots of 2 s, so 3 × 3 = 9 m.
Its position stays the same while time passes.
